name: Rice & Grains
summary: Water ratios and times for rice and common grains, the stovetop method, and storing cooked rice safely.

items: Rinse white rice in a sieve until the water runs mostly clear; it washes off loose starch so the grains don't clump. Quinoa needs a rinse too, to remove its bitter coating.
Put the grain, water and a pinch of salt in a pot with a tight lid and bring to a boil.
Turn the heat to low, cover, and simmer without lifting the lid for the time below.
Take it off the heat and let it sit, still covered, for 10 minutes. Then fluff with a fork.

sections.heading: Ratios and times
blocks: Water is per 1 cup of dry grain. One cup of dry rice (about 185–200 g) makes about 3 cups cooked, enough for 3–4 people as a side.

rows: 1 ¼ cups (300 ml) boiling water, poured over

blocks.text: Brown rice, farro and barley can also be boiled in a big pot of salted water like pasta, then drained. It's harder to get wrong, and the ratio stops mattering.

sections.heading: Rice cookers
blocks: A rice cooker does the timing and keeps rice warm. Use the cup that came with it (usually smaller than a US cup, about ¾ cup (180 ml)) and fill water to the line for that number of cups.

sections.heading: Cooked rice safety

blocks.text: Cooked rice can carry spores of Bacillus cereus that survive cooking and multiply at room temperature. Refrigerate leftover rice within 1–2 hours, spread out to cool quickly, eat it within 3–4 days, and reheat until steaming hot.

blocks: Day-old, cold rice makes the best fried rice: it's drier, so the grains stay separate.
